newsitem.title: DUBAI: FEATURE - Gulf states seen dragging feet on privatisation.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Gulf states seen dragging feet on privatisation.

text.p: Privatisation seems to be the talk of the town in Gulf Arab states but the private sector train appears to be stuck in the oil-rich desert sands.

"So far there has been no fundamental effort towards privatisation in all Gulf states," Kuwaiti economist Jassem al-Saadoun told Reuters. "Privatisation is a must for the economy. It is no longer an option."
The six nations that make up the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and sit on 40 percent of world oil reserves want the private sector to play a bigger role in the state-orchestrated, welfare economies.

After years of budget deficits -- a result of hefty spending amid low oil prices until early 1996 -- they want to shift some responsibility for economic growth on to the private sector and reduce their vulnerability to mercurial oil earnings.
Yet they are moving too slowly to lure private cash by overhauling laws on financial transparency and easing curbs on foreign investment, economists and businessmen say.
Oil will remain the driving force behind economies and state spending will prop up development projects, they say.
They believe the GCC will never follow the Western example of governments selling all their shares in public institutions.
Instead, most will invite the private sector to take part in future capital expansion projects, including oil and power and water, to meet increasing demand from a growing population.
"You will never see a total sell-off of companies owned by governments in the GCC," Saudi economist Ihsan Bu-Hulaiga said.
PRIVATE SECTOR MIGHT LACK EXPERIENCE
Many fear the private sector in Gulf Arab states might lack the experience to run huge projects. Massive long-term funding, from local banks and through bonds, remains scarce.

"The GCC governments understand they have to relinquish control over certain facilities to the private sector. They have nothing against that. This will be gradual. It will never be from zero to 100 degrees overnight as the private sector has to be tested," Bu-Hulaiga said.

"In general, the GCC is not in need of cash. What they are interested in is to maximise or enlarge the investment flow into their respective economies and one way of doing that is to give additional opportunities to private sector investments."

Apart from a few free trade zones, foreign firms are limited to 49 percent ownership in most states. Foreign investment is also limited in Gulf equity markets, where some 300 shares are listed and turnover is slim -- one-fifth of Singapore's.
Some industries are heavily protected and state utilities subsidised and in most Gulf Arab states family-owned enterprises continue to serve as agents for everything.
Recently stronger oil prices have showered Gulf states with more petrodollars and helped ease deficits. But these will only provide a cosmetic boost to regional economies.
GCC STATES APPEAR GENUINE ABOUT PRIVATISATION
While some GCC states are making more headway than others on privatisation, economists agree they remain genuine about it.
In Kuwait, officials hope parliament will soon pass a privatisation law to help kick off a plan to shed state involvement in some public utilities and services during 1997.

Its privatisation plan aims at selling stakes in about 60 firms and preparing for a second and more difficult phase to end state involvement in some public services such as water, electricity and telecommunications.
It has sold state assets in 17 local firms worth 650 million dinars ($2.17 billion) since the 1991 Gulf War.
Oman, which is not as wealthy as its northern neighbours but further down the privatisation road, is preparing for the privatisation of its profitable telecommunications company.
Sultan Qaboos bin Said has set up a ministerial committee to handle privatisation in Oman.

It became the first Gulf Arab state to issue a build, own, operate, transfer (BOOT) scheme for an infrastructure project when the Manah power station came on stream in April. It also plans to use BOOT in Muscat and Salalah waste water projects.
In Saudi Arabia, by far the largest Gulf Arab economy, the first utility company with foreign and private participation is set to be operational later this year. But more still needs to be done.
Its 1995-2000 development plan focuses on privatisation and promises the government will not get into any activity "that the private sector can finance, run or manage".

Privatisation of certain state assets, including the sale of state holdings in telephones, railways, electricity, education services and 37 firms on the Saudi stock market could raise about 100 billion riyals ($26.7 billion), some economists say.
QATAR, BAHRAIN, UAE APPEAR TO BE DRAGGING THEIR FEET
Qatar, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) appear to be dragging their feet in boosting the private sector role, economists say.
Qatar offers the most promise for foreign investors because of its lucrative gas projects and willingness to allow foreign companies to take a leading role in its energy projects.
Doha, with foreign companies, is pumping more than $10 billion into liquefied natural gas projects.

In the UAE, Abu Dhabi has set up a committee to oversee privatisation of water and electricity, but economists say the oil-rich country will find it difficult to wean its people off the generous welfare system.

Bahrain, scene of sporadic unrest since 1994, has no clear privatisation plan and needs to embark on structural adjustment measures, economists say. It has sold stakes in a food factory and a downstream aluminium plant.
